questions.question: What is the closed metric ball $\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)$?
options: $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{X}\colon d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0) \lt r\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{X}\colon d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0) \gt r\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{X}\colon d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0)\leq r\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\boldsymbol{X}\colon d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0) = 0\}$

questions.question: What does the bar in $\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)$ indicate here?
options: A closed metric ball.
An open metric ball.
A ball with no centre.
A subset containing only boundary points.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the usual distance, which condition describes membership in $\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}((0,0),1)$?
What topological property does a closed metric ball always have?
options: The closed metric ball is always an open set.
The closed metric ball is always empty.
The closed metric ball never contains its centre.
The closed metric ball is a closed set.

questions.question: Let $r = 2$. Which point lies in $\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}((0,0),2)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the usual distance?
In $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the usual distance, why is $(1,0)$ in $\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}((0,0),1)$?
options: Its distance from $(0,0)$ is greater than $1$.
Its distance from $(0,0)$ is exactly $1$, which closed balls include.
Closed balls exclude the points whose distance is exactly equal to the radius.
It is in the ball only because every point of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is in it.

questions.question: Which statement correctly reflects the warning about general metric spaces?
options: In every metric space, the closed metric ball is always the closure of the corresponding open metric ball.
In a general metric space, closed balls are never closed sets.
In a general metric space, the closed metric ball need not equal the closure of the corresponding open metric ball.
In a general metric space, closed balls cannot contain their centres.

questions.question: Which assumption is needed for the closure statement about open balls to be safely applied?
options: The radius is negative.
Under the Euclidean or an equivalent metric.
The centre lies outside the whole metric space.
The closed ball is empty.

questions.question: In the discrete metric on a set with at least two points, take radius $r = 1$ around $\boldsymbol{x}_0$. Which statement illustrates the general-metric warning?
options: Closed ball may be $X$; open ball closure is $\{\boldsymbol{x}_0\}$.
The closed ball must be empty.
The open ball of radius $1$ must contain all points.
The closure of the open ball must contain no points.

questions.question: In a metric space $(X,d)$, let $x,x_0\in X$ and $r>0$ satisfy $d(x,x_0)=r$. Which statement about membership of $x$ in the closed ball centred at $x_0$ with radius $r$ is correct?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}$ is excluded from the closed ball.
$\boldsymbol{x}\in\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)$.
$\boldsymbol{x}$ is outside $\boldsymbol{X}$.
The radius must be $0$.

questions.question: Which set-theoretic property holds for every closed metric ball?
options: It is always open and not closed.
It is always empty.
It is a closed set.
It is always the whole space.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^2$, is $(2,0)$ in $\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}((0,0),1)$?
options: Yes, because it lies on an axis.
Yes, because closed balls contain all points.
No, because the origin is excluded.
No, its distance from the origin is $2$.

questions.question: What warning is given for closed balls in general metric spaces?
options: A closed ball need not equal the closure of the open ball.
A closed metric ball is never closed.
A closed metric ball is always empty.
A closed metric ball cannot be defined by means of the metric $d$.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the usual distance, does $(1,1)$ belong to $\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}((0,0),\sqrt{2})$?
options: No, because equality with the radius is excluded.
No, because closed balls contain only axis points.
Yes, because its distance from the origin is $\sqrt{2}$.
Yes, because every point has distance $0$.
